data.title: Mercedes-Benz Wins German Approval For Point-To-Point Driving Assistance
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - Mercedes-Benz Group AG (MBG.DE, MBG.MI, MBGYY, MBGAF) on Friday said it has become the first automaker to receive German regulatory approval for a point-to-point driving assistance system.

The company's SAE Level 2 MB.DRIVE ASSIST PRO system supports drivers throughout journeys, including complex urban traffic, following approval by Germany's Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA).

The approval was granted under the requirements of UN Regulation No. 171, which establishes safety standards for Driver Control Assistance Systems (DCAS). The harmonized regulatory framework is expected to take effect in January 2027, potentially enabling the technology's introduction in other markets where the regulation applies.

Mercedes-Benz plans to launch an Early Access Programme in Stuttgart and Munich in December 2026, allowing selected customers to test the features and provide feedback.

A broader rollout across Germany is planned for the first half of 2027, covering passenger cars and vans across all powertrain types. Owners of eligible vehicles will also be able to add the functions through an over-the-air update.

data.title: Williams CEO Chad Zamarin Urges House Action Following Senate Passage of Bipartisan Permitting Reform
data.description:
Chad Zamarin, President and CEO of Williams () released the following statement following the U.S. Senate’s passing of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) of 2026:

“The Senate’s passage of BAAJA is an important win for American families and American energy, and now the House has an opportunity to finish the job. We thank Senators Capito, Lee, Heinrich and Whitehouse for working together to advance meaningful, bipartisan permitting reform.

America has the energy, the resources and the capital to build. What we’ve lacked is a permitting system that lets us get it done. The BAAJA can change that, helping deliver the infrastructure we need to lower costs and meet rapidly growing energy demand.

Nowhere is that problem clearer than in the Northeast. During last winter’s cold snap, energy prices in New England spiked by more than 10 times the normal cost because the region simply does not have enough infrastructure to reliably access abundant and affordable American energy. Projects that could help solve that problem have been delayed or blocked for years.

BAAJA takes an important step toward lowering costs for Americans by bringing greater certainty and accountability to the permitting process. That means getting critical energy infrastructure built, strengthening reliability and helping lower energy bills for American families.

We urge the House to act quickly, pass BAAJA and get America back to building.”

About Williams

Williams () is a trusted energy industry leader committed to safely, reliably and responsibly meeting growing energy demand. We use our infrastructure to deliver one third of the nation’s natural gas to where it's needed most, supplying the energy used to heat our homes, cook our food and generate low-carbon electricity. For over a century, we’ve been driven by a passion for doing things the right way. Today, our team of problem solvers is leading the charge into the clean energy future. Learn more at www.williams.com.

data.title: Wall St slides on mounting AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow set to confirm corrections
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indexes: Dow down 0.57%, S&P 500 off 2.06%, Nasdaq down 3.40%
  • Anthropic down 10.2% a day after debut
  • Intuit down after company cuts revenue forecast, agrees to sell unit
  • Caterpillar falls amid demand concerns for its AI-related energy generation equipment

By Stephen Culp and Utkarsh Hathi

US stocks extended their rout on Friday, putting the S&P 500 and the Dow on course to confirm corrections after Anthropic's momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries over the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally.

All three major US equity indexes were sharply lower, with the Dow and the S&P 500 now more than 10% below their record closing highs reached on October 6. Should those levels hold, it would confirm both indexes entered corrections on that date.

The bellwether S&P 500 is poised to notch its seventh consecutive drop, which would mark its longest losing streak since February 2020.

All three indexes are on track to log their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling "liberation day" tariff package.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq entered negative territory for the year.

"The question that lingers is are we in a bear market or not?" said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. "This feels more to me like a correction within a bull market, which tend to be very violent and fast."

Anthropic's supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as $2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch fire on Thursday, closing 17.1% above its $83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.

The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia's quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.

In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic's shares were down 10.2%.

"Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate earnings history; they did everything right," Carlson added. "A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn't."

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index , which has powered much of the broader stock market's gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6% in mid-June. That luster has faded, with the index's year-to-date advance having shrunk to 21.4%.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon was off 3.1%, while Meta dropped 4.7%.

Neocloud firms CoreWeave and Nebius slid over 10% each.

The tech selloff has prompted a rotation into more defensive sectors such as staples and healthcare , which were up 1.5% and 0.7%, respectively.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 278.99 points, or 0.57%, to 48,818.07, the S&P 500 CBOE:SPX lost 147.76 points, or 2.06%, to 7,028.07 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 810.98 points, or 3.40%, to 23,068.22.

INFLATION, FED IN FOCUS

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank's policy rate is not high enough to deal with inflation levels.

Markets are pricing in a 95.5% chance of an interest rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

A report from the University of Michigan survey showed post-election consumer sentiment rose to 7.3%.

Next week's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed's monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 10.8% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much.

UnitedHealth rose 4.7% after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a "buy" from a "hold" rating.

The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 3.6% lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.27-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 32 new highs and 965 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 1,208 stocks rose and 3,563 fell as declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.95-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 18 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 13 new highs and 692 new lows.

data.title: The Fed is too busy fighting inflation to rescue the stock market
data.description:
By Greg Robb

Concern about financial condition seems to favor a gradual pace of rate hikes

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks at his press conference in October.

The U.S. stock market plunged this week into correction territory, with the major indexes down more than 10% from recent highs, but don't expect the U.S. central bank to come to the rescue.

Federal Reserve officials will continue to raise interest rates, despite the recent selloff in the stock market, as equity-market gains over the past four years dwarf the recent declines, economists said Friday.

"We would need a much larger retreat in equity values to make a dent in the wealth that has been generated by the stock market over the prior few years," said Avery Shenfeld, chief economist of CIBC Capital Markets.

Scott Anderson, chief U.S. economist at BMO Capital Markets agreed: "People have done so well over the past several years. There is some room for stocks to fall without all consumers stopping spending and air traffic going down."

Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon, said most Fed officials are looking through the stock-market volatility.

"Regardless of the fact that financial conditions have tightened, they will still want to signal and implement a tighter monetary stance," Daco said.

The Fed raised rates a quarter-point in September, the first increase in three years, in an effort to battle the persistent upward creep of consumer prices.

Officials made no change to rates in October, in part because the stock market was weak, according to minutes of the Fed meeting released Wednesday. At the same time, almost all Fed officials anticipated further rate hikes.

CIBC's Shenfeld said there are two reasons why stocks would matter for the Fed: if the market falls far enough to cause negative wealth effects, or if the market is a predictor of where the economy is going.

That's less likely to be true after the huge run-up of the past few years, he said.

"At this point, I don't think it is material for them. It can become material, but we're not there yet," Shenfeld added. The S&P 500 SPX is clinging to positive gains in 2026 and has returned 100% over the past four years.

Fed officials are focused on the risks to the economy and markets from a reversal of optimism surrounding AI. Minutes of their October meeting disclosed that officials had lengthy discussions over various scenarios surrounding a possible market selloff.

"They are starting to get serious about what their playbook would be if this would get worse," Anderson said. The biggest worry would be "systemic dislocation" in financial markets, he added.

That might require the Fed to set up special credit lines to inject liquidity into markets, similar to actions taken in the financial crisis of 2008 and the dawn of the COVID pandemic in 2020, Anderson said.

At the moment, the Fed might be breathing "a sigh of relief" over the recent stock-market drop because it is concerned about high stock valuations and related hedge-fund leverage. A modest decline in equities "lets some the air out of the balloon," Anderson said.

Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide Financial, said if the Fed skips a hike in December, they would be accused of putting a floor under stock prices - in other words, "a Fed put" - a charge that has dogged the central bank since the late 1980s.

How bad would the stock-market selloff does have to get before the Fed changes their thinking about interest rates?

Officials will keep an eye on bank distress and distress in the plumbing of financial markets as signs that there may be more trouble lurking, Anderson said.

For now, a hike in December is seen as a done deal given the hot October inflation readings. After that, the future direction of the Fed becomes more of an open question.

Concerns about financial conditions seem to favor a gradual pace of hikes, meaning the Fed pausing at its January meeting and hiking again in March, wrote Michael Gapen, chief U.S. economist at Morgan Stanley, in a note to clients.

Many economist have penciled in a more aggressive rate path, with the Fed hiking three times - in December, January and March, before pausing to assess conditions. Shenfeld said he expects two hikes, one next month and another in January.

"I think they are worried about inflation getting ingrained at 3% as opposed to 2%, which is why they are willing to put a bit of a dent into growth to pull inflation down," Shenfeld said.

A modest slowdown in growth coupled with lower oil prices could take a lot of the wind out of inflation, he added.

Some economists are worried that the Fed will overtighten, and are blinded by concern that they haven't hit their 2% inflation target in almost six years.

"Markets are signaling that the current level of interest rates is unsustainably high," wrote Andrew Hollenhorst, U.S. chief economist at Citi, who is one of the most dovish economists on Wall Street.

A rate hike remains likely early next month, but then the Fed will stay on hold and eventually cut later next year, he said in a note to clients.

-Greg Robb

data.title: Alphabet just overtook Nvidia in market value for the first time in over 2 years
data.description:
By Christine Ji

Nvidia is now the fourth-most valuable U.S. company, behind Apple, Microsoft and Alphabet

Alphabet's launch of a new Gemini 4 model this week gave the stock a boost.

A deepening selloff in Nvidia shares has sent the chip maker sliding down the ranks of the largest U.S. companies.

Alphabet (GOOGL) (GOOG) is the latest company to overtake Nvidia (NVDA) in terms of market capitalization, leading Nvidia to fall to fourth place behind the Google parent company. Apple (AAPL) is now the world's largest company, followed by Microsoft (MSFT).

Shares of Nvidia were down 6.9% in Friday trading, bringing the company's market capitalization to $3.260 trillion. Shares of Alphabet, on the other hand, were up 0.4%. Alphabet currently has a market capitalization of $3.323 trillion.

The last time Alphabet commanded a higher valuation than Nvidia, as well as the last time Nvidia sat fourth or lower on the U.S. leaderboard, was April 19, 2024, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

The shake-up comes as Nvidia shares head for their seventh straight week of losses. The stock has fallen over 40% from its 52-week high of $243.37 a share back in early October as the company deals with heightened regulatory scrutiny surrounding its business dealings in Southeast Asia. Following former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, Wall Street is also concerned about the company's long-term succession plan.

The Wall Street Journal reported earlier this week that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has opened a civil probe into Nvidia's investor disclosures. And on Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia.

Not even an earnings beat and an optimistic outlook from earlier in the week could stem the selloff. Nvidia posted record quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier.

"Nvidia's leadership uncertainty adds another layer of risk, and the stock's weakness despite strong earnings shows how much it will take to restore confidence," David Miller, CIO and portfolio manager at Catalyst Funds, wrote in a Friday note.

Meanwhile, Alphabet has received a boost of confidence following new artificial-intelligence developments. On Wednesday, Google rolled out its Gemini 4 Neon model, aimed at complex software coding, scientific research and multistep business tasks.

In a Friday note, J.P. Morgan analyst Doug Anmuth highlighted Alphabet's increased launch cadence as a sign that the company is gaining ground in the AI race. Neon is the company's fourth Gemini 4 model in two months.

-Christine Ji
